title: Geospatial Reconnaissance (GEOINT/IMINT) and Shadow Geometry
intro: A single photograph contains infinite environmental clues: the angle of sunlight, the height of a light pole, the gauge of a railroad track, the shape of a mountain ridge. When metadata is stripped, physics and geography take over.

sections.heading: 1. Turning Pixels into Coordinates: The GEOINT Triangulation Mindset
sections.content:
Imagine you are handed an image with zero EXIF data. The image shows an industrial building with a white truck parked out front. Amateurs give up. Intelligence analysts look closer.

*Where do we look first?*
1. **Infrastructure Clues:** Look at power transmission lines. Are the towers lattice steel, single pole, or wooden? Are the electrical sockets inside the building Type A (US), Type C (EU), or Type G (UK)?
2. **Transportation & Signage:** Look at road markings. Are the lines yellow or white? Which side of the road are cars driving on? What is the font on the highway exit sign?
3. **Natural Features:** Mountain topography, vegetation biomes (e.g. palm trees vs boreal pines), soil color (red clay vs dark loam).

When you combine two distinct landmark bearings—say, a church spire and a radio broadcast tower visible in the background—you can draw lines of sight on Google Earth Pro. Where those lines intersect is the exact camera viewpoint.

sections.heading: 2. Chronolocation: Shadow Geometry & SunCalc
sections.content:
Did you know that shadows are nature's clock and calendar?

If you know the height of an object (or can estimate it relative to a person or standard door) and measure the length of the shadow it casts on flat ground, you can calculate the **solar elevation angle** using basic trigonometry:
`tan(Elevation Angle) = Object Height / Shadow Length`.

Now, look at the direction the shadow is pointing. If the shadow points directly North-Northwest, the sun was located South-Southeast (solar azimuth ~150°).

*Where do we pivot next?*
We input the estimated geographic region into tools like **SunCalc** (suncalc.org) or **PeakVisor**. By sliding the time of day and calendar date sliders, you match the exact sun elevation and azimuth to the minute. You have just achieved **Chronolocation**: proving not only where the photo was taken, but the exact hour and season it occurred.

sections.heading: 3. Satellite Imagery & Change Detection
sections.content:
Commercial satellite constellations (Sentinel-2, Planet Labs, Maxar) pass over every square meter of the Earth every few days.

Using platforms like **Sentinel Hub EO Browser** or **Google Earth historical imagery slider**, analysts perform **Change Detection**:
- Has a new fence or security checkpoint appeared outside a suspected black site between March and June?
- Has a trench been dug? Has asphalt been freshly poured?
- Are thermal signatures or infrared vegetation indices (NDVI) showing stressed crops or underground pipeline heat leaks?

When you master GEOINT, the physical world becomes an open book.
